stances.claim: For the culture of integrity to succeed, it must permeate not just big corporations but the entire business community -- especially SMEs which are 99.6% of all businesses.
Petty graft has been so normalized that it no longer outrages -- this acceptance is what makes corruption flourish and multiply ever more.
PCCI is the undisputed champion of SMEs and should match the big leaguers by launching an anti-corruption drive among grassroots enterprises.
stances.rhetorical_move: direct challenge to a named institution

notable_anecdotes: The fire extinguisher racket: fire department inspectors requiring SMEs to buy from a recommended 'pre-cleared' supplier list -- a concrete example of petty graft embedded in regulatory compliance.
Sari-sari store owners having to bribe municipal functionaries for operating permits -- the most intimate, everyday form of petty corruption.

The verbal resistance scripts: 'My company has a very strict policy against bribes, and I would lose my job if I violate it' and 'It is against my religion to pay bribes' -- practical tools for individual SME owners.
target_audience: PCCI President Francis Chua and PCCI leadership
Business associations below the big-league level
decision_framework_signals: Apply the seven AIM practices as a minimum anti-corruption compliance checklist for any SME
Train employees on verbal resistance scripts for bribe demand situations
Use accurate tax compliance as a structural defense against extortion -- correct taxpayers have less vulnerability
Treat normalization of facilitation payments as the primary enemy -- zero tolerance must be culturally enforced, not just legally mandated
one_paragraph_summary: Following the big-business Integrity Initiative (Makati Business Club, MAP, ECCI, AmCham, AIM Hills Program), Panganiban argues that the culture of integrity must reach the grassroots: SMEs (micro/small/medium enterprises) constitute 99.6% of all businesses, employ 63.2% of the labor force, and account for 35.7% of total sales -- yet are the favorite victims of petty grafters. The column catalogs normalized petty-corruption examples: bribes for sari-sari permits, health clearances, customs releases, tax assessment reductions, fire-extinguisher rackets from 'pre-cleared' suppliers, and traffic violations. The AIM Hills Program on Governance recommends seven practices: (1) prohibit bribery in any form, communicated to all stakeholders; (2) gifts/entertainment policy with nominal-value limits and a central register; (3) conflict-of-interest disclosure form; (4) Code of Conduct with incentives and penalties; (5) periodic anti-corruption training from hire; (6) transparent systems, accurate books, official receipts; and (7) correct tax declarations, using verbal scripts to resist bribe demands ('My company has a very strict policy' / 'It is against my religion to pay bribes'). The column closes with a direct challenge to PCCI president Francis Chua -- who accepted in response to last Sunday's column -- to launch an SME anti-corruption drive at the PCCI national conference.
